case_name: Gaya Prasad Ramlal v State of Maharashtra
respondent:
State of Maharashtra
Supreme Court of India

1 March 1971
Cr.A. No. 204 of 1968 (Cri. Appl. No. 841 of 1966, D/- 16 February 1968 - Bom.), Dt. 1 March 1971.
The Judgment was delivered by: RAY, J.
1. This is an appeal by special leave from the judgment dated 16 February, 1968 of the High Court of Bombay convicting the appellant u/s. 302 read with S. 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The Sessions Judge tried the appellant under Sections 143, 147, 148, 302 and 306 read with S. 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court convicted accused Nos. 1, 2 and 5 u/s. 302 read with S. 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for life. The High Court convicted accused Nos. 2, 3 and 6 u/s. 326 read with S. 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced each of them to rigorous imprisonment for three years. The sentence of accused No. 2 was to run concurrently.

facts: This is an appeal by special leave from the judgment dated 16 February, 1968 of the High Court of Bombay convicting the appellant u/s. 302 read with S. 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
The Sessions Judge tried the appellant under Sections 143, 147, 148, 302 and 306 read with S. 149 of the Indian Penal Code.
Accused No. 1 Habib Ahmed, accused No. 2 Maksood Ahmed and accused No. 6 Mohmood Ahmed are brothers.
Phelwan was absconding since the date of the offence.
Gaya Prasad alias Chakkiwala, accused No. 5 was the owner of a flour mill and was referred to by all the witnesses as Chakkiwala
Accused No. 1 lived in a house Masjid Chawl at Khar in Greater Bombay.
Rashidkhan the deceased in the present appeal along with a few other persons of the locality passed a resolution that accused No. 1 should not be permitted to live in a part of the Masjid.
About two months before date of the incident 16 August, 1965 accused No. 2, the brother of accused No. 1, borrowed a sliver bracelet from Hanisuddin Saifulla.
On 15th August, 1965, accused No. 2 called on Hanisuddin.
He asked for the return of the bracelet.
Accused No. 2 refused to return it and instead brandished a knife.
Hanisuddin went to the police station and lodged a compliant.
On 16th August, 1965 accused No. 2 again went to Hanisuddin's hut at about 9 p.m.
Accused No. 1 returned to the open place with a knife in his hand.
He was followed by the appellant accused No. 5 and finding that Rashid was standing in the open space between the two Chawls accused No. 5 gave a shout 'maro, maro'.
Accused No. 1 then gave two blows with a knife on the buttocks of Rashid.
Phelwan also assaulted Rashid with a knife.
Mehmoodkhan who saw the assault on Rashid, tried to go to his help.
Sunder Anna another absconding accused engaged Mehmoodkhan in a struggle.
While the struggle was going on accused No. 2 attacked Rashid with a knife.
Accused Nos. 3 and 6 came on the scene and were armed with stripped stick and iron pipe respectively.
They assaulted Mehmoodkhan repeatedly.
So did accused No. 4 who was armed with a stick with a knob on.
Accused No. 3 pulled out a pipe from the roof of Rashid's house and gave a blow on the face of Rashid with that pipe and Phelwan gave a final blow on his back.
issues: Whether the evidence that the appellant shouted 'maro maro' was not free from doubt.

Whether assuming that the appellant was present, he did not carry any weapon and arms and he had no motive and on the facts it could not be said that between accused No. 1 and accused No. 5 there was any prior meeting for a pre-conceived plan and therefore there was no common intention.
petitioner_arguments: The evidence that the appellant shouted 'maro maro' was not free from doubt.

Assuming that the appellant was present, he did not carry any weapon and arms and he had no motive and on the facts it could not be said that between accused No. 1 and accused No. 5 there was any prior meeting for a pre-conceived plan and therefore there was no common intention.
respondent_arguments: The evidence found by the High Court is that Rashidkhan and Mehmoodkhan were assaulted at a place which was a narrow open space surrounded by huts on all sides in the colony except for the two small openings in the east and the west.
The attack on Rashidkhan was not unpremeditated.
The suddenness is accentuated by the shout given by the appellant.
court_reasoning: As to the appellant there is the consistent testimony of each of the eye-witnesses that the incident commenced with the appellant shouting 'maro, maro'.

There is evidence to show that accused No. 1 was armed with a knife and the lead which accused No. 5, the appellant gave establishes that accused No. 1 should commence the attack on Rashidkhan with a knife.
The result is that accused No. 5, the appellant, shared in intention of accused Nos. 1 and 2 to commit the murder of Rashidkhan.
holding: The judgment of the High Court is correct.
There is no merit in this appeal.
The appeal fails and is dismissed.
